claim: SHP2 is a protein tyrosine phosphatase that normally potentiates intracellular signaling by growth factors, antigen receptors, and some cytokines.
source: SHP2 is a protein tyrosine phosphatase that normally potentiates intracellular signaling by growth factors, antigen receptors, and some cytokines, yet is frequently mutated in human cancer.
evidence: This is established knowledge about SHP2 function in the field.

claim: SHP2 is frequently mutated in human cancer.
source: SHP2 is a protein tyrosine phosphatase that normally potentiates intracellular signaling by growth factors, antigen receptors, and some cytokines, yet is frequently mutated in human cancer.
evidence: This is established knowledge about SHP2 in cancer.

claim: The dynamics of phosphotyrosine abundance at more than 400 tyrosine residues reveal six distinct response signatures following SHP099 treatment and washout.
source: The dynamics of phosphotyrosine abundance at more than 400 tyrosine residues reveal six distinct response signatures following SHP099 treatment and washout.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the phosphoproteomics data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Occludin contains newly identified SHP2 substrate sites.
source: Remarkably, in addition to newly identified substrate sites on proteins such as occludin, ARHGAP35, and PLCγ2, another class of sites shows reduced phosphotyrosine abundance upon SHP2 inhibition.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the phosphoproteomics and validation experiments.

claim: ARHGAP35 contains newly identified SHP2 substrate sites.
source: Remarkably, in addition to newly identified substrate sites on proteins such as occludin, ARHGAP35, and PLCγ2, another class of sites shows reduced phosphotyrosine abundance upon SHP2 inhibition.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the phosphoproteomics and validation experiments.

claim: PLCγ2 contains newly identified SHP2 substrate sites.
source: Remarkably, in addition to newly identified substrate sites on proteins such as occludin, ARHGAP35, and PLCγ2, another class of sites shows reduced phosphotyrosine abundance upon SHP2 inhibition.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the phosphoproteomics and validation experiments.

claim: A class of sites shows reduced phosphotyrosine abundance upon SHP2 inhibition.
source: Remarkably, in addition to newly identified substrate sites on proteins such as occludin, ARHGAP35, and PLCγ2, another class of sites shows reduced phosphotyrosine abundance upon SHP2 inhibition.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the phosphoproteomics data.

claim: Sites of decreased phospho-abundance are enriched on proteins with two nearby phosphotyrosine residues.
source: Sites of decreased phospho-abundance are enriched on proteins with two nearby phosphotyrosine residues, which can be directly protected from dephosphorylation by the paired SH2 domains of SHP2 itself.
evidence: This is a finding from analysis of the phosphoproteomics data.

claim: Sites with two nearby phosphotyrosine residues can be directly protected from dephosphorylation by the paired SH2 domains of SHP2.
source: Sites of decreased phospho-abundance are enriched on proteins with two nearby phosphotyrosine residues, which can be directly protected from dephosphorylation by the paired SH2 domains of SHP2 itself.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data with SHP2 domain mutants.

claim: SHP2 has distinct roles in scaffolding and catalytic activities in effecting a transmembrane signaling response.
source: These findings highlight the distinct roles of the scaffolding and catalytic activities of SHP2 in effecting a transmembrane signaling response.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the phosphoproteomics and mutational data.

claim: SHP2 is essential for mammalian development.
source: SHP2 is a non-receptor tyrosine phosphatase that is essential for mammalian development (Saxton et al., 1997).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Germline mutations of PTPN11 cause Noonan syndrome.
source: In humans, germline mutations of PTPN11 cause the developmental disorders Noonan and LEOPARD syndromes (Tartaglia and Gelb, 2005).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Germline mutations of PTPN11 cause LEOPARD syndrome.
source: In humans, germline mutations of PTPN11 cause the developmental disorders Noonan and LEOPARD syndromes (Tartaglia and Gelb, 2005).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Somatic PTPN11 activating mutations are found frequently in juvenile myelomonocytic leukemia.
source: Somatic PTPN11 activating mutations are also found frequently in juvenile myelomonocytic leukemia and, to a lesser extent, in solid tumors (Bentires-Alj et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Somatic PTPN11 activating mutations are found to a lesser extent in solid tumors.
source: Somatic PTPN11 activating mutations are also found frequently in juvenile myelomonocytic leukemia and, to a lesser extent, in solid tumors (Bentires-Alj et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: SHP2 acts as a positive effector of receptor tyrosine kinase (RTK) signaling.
source: Numerous studies have shown that SHP2 acts as a positive effector of receptor tyrosine kinase (RTK) signaling (Bennett et al., 1994; Easton et al., 2006; Tang et al., 1995).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: SHP2 facilitates the full induction of Ras-dependent extracellular signal-regulated kinase (ERK) proteins following stimulation of cells with epidermal growth factor (EGF).
source: SHP2 facilitates the full induction of Ras-dependent extracellular signal-regulated kinase (ERK) proteins following stimulation of cells with epidermal growth factor (EGF) or other receptor tyrosine kinase ligands.
evidence: This is established knowledge about SHP2 function.

claim: SHP2 facilitates the full induction of Ras-dependent extracellular signal-regulated kinase (ERK) proteins following stimulation of cells with other receptor tyrosine kinase ligands.
source: SHP2 facilitates the full induction of Ras-dependent extracellular signal-regulated kinase (ERK) proteins following stimulation of cells with epidermal growth factor (EGF) or other receptor tyrosine kinase ligands.
evidence: This is established knowledge about SHP2 function.

claim: SHP2 serves as a positive regulator of cytokine signaling systems.
source: SHP2 also serves as a positive regulator of numerous other signaling systems, including cytokine (Xu and Qu, 2008), programmed cell death (Yokosuka et al., 2012), and immune checkpoint pathways (Gavrieli et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: SHP2 serves as a positive regulator of programmed cell death pathways.
source: SHP2 also serves as a positive regulator of numerous other signaling systems, including cytokine (Xu and Qu, 2008), programmed cell death (Yokosuka et al., 2012), and immune checkpoint pathways (Gavrieli et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: SHP2 serves as a positive regulator of immune checkpoint pathways.
source: SHP2 also serves as a positive regulator of numerous other signaling systems, including cytokine (Xu and Qu, 2008), programmed cell death (Yokosuka et al., 2012), and immune checkpoint pathways (Gavrieli et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: The SHP2 protein consists of two SH2 domains (N-SH2, C-SH2), followed by a phosphatase (PTP) domain, with a natively disordered C-terminal tail that contains tyrosine residues known to become phosphorylated.
source: The SHP2 protein consists of two SH2 domains (N-SH2, C-SH2), followed by a phosphatase (PTP) domain, with a natively disordered C-terminal tail that contains tyrosine residues known to become phosphorylated (Bennett et al., 1994; Keegan and Cooper, 1996).
evidence: This is established knowledge about SHP2 structure, supported by citations.

claim: Wild-type SHP2 normally adopts an autoinhibited conformation in which the N-SH2 domain occludes the active site of the PTP domain.
source: X-ray structures of the SHP2 protein core, encompassing the two SH2 domains and the PTP domain, show that the wild-type protein normally adopts an autoinhibited conformation in which the N-SH2 domain occludes the active site of the PTP domain (Hof et al., 1998).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to structural studies.

claim: Activation of SHP2 requires disengagement of the N-SH2 domain from the PTP domain.
source: Activation of the enzyme requires disengagement of the N-SH2 domain from the PTP domain and subsequent recruitment of SHP2 to phosphotyrosine docking sites on substrate proteins.
evidence: This is established knowledge about SHP2 activation mechanism.

claim: Activation of SHP2 requires subsequent recruitment of SHP2 to phosphotyrosine docking sites on substrate proteins.
source: Activation of the enzyme requires disengagement of the N-SH2 domain from the PTP domain and subsequent recruitment of SHP2 to phosphotyrosine docking sites on substrate proteins.
evidence: This is established knowledge about SHP2 activation mechanism.

claim: Recruitment of SHP2 can rely on the N-SH2 domain, C-SH2 domain, or both domains.
source: Recruitment can rely on the N-SH2 domain, C-SH2 domain, or both domains.
evidence: This is established knowledge about SHP2 recruitment mechanisms.

claim: Most oncogenic mutations of SHP2 lie at the interface between the N-SH2 and PTP domains.
source: Most oncogenic mutations of SHP2 lie at the interface between the N-SH2 and PTP domains, thereby increasing the propensity of the enzyme to adopt an open, active conformation (LaRochelle et al., 2018; LaRochelle et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Oncogenic mutations of SHP2 increase the propensity of the enzyme to adopt an open, active conformation.
source: Most oncogenic mutations of SHP2 lie at the interface between the N-SH2 and PTP domains, thereby increasing the propensity of the enzyme to adopt an open, active conformation (LaRochelle et al., 2018; LaRochelle et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: GAB1 and GAB2 are adaptor proteins thought to recruit SHP2 to sites of active signaling following RTK activation.
source: Numerous studies in a range of cell types have identified phosphotyrosine (pY) residues on adaptor proteins (e.g. GAB1 and GAB2 [Arnaud et al., 2004; Cunnick et al., 2001]) or on RTKs themselves (e.g. PDGFβR [Rönnstrand et al., 1999]) thought to recruit SHP2 to sites of active signaling following RTK activation (such sites include multiprotein complexes formed on RTK intracellular tails and IRS-1 adapters).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: PDGFβR is thought to recruit SHP2 to sites of active signaling following RTK activation.
source: Numerous studies in a range of cell types have identified phosphotyrosine (pY) residues on adaptor proteins (e.g. GAB1 and GAB2 [Arnaud et al., 2004; Cunnick et al., 2001]) or on RTKs themselves (e.g. PDGFβR [Rönnstrand et al., 1999]) thought to recruit SHP2 to sites of active signaling following RTK activation (such sites include multiprotein complexes formed on RTK intracellular tails and IRS-1 adapters).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Genetic and mutational studies have implicated specific pY residues on RTKs as putative SHP2 substrates.
source: Genetic and mutational studies have implicated specific pY residues on RTKs as putative SHP2 substrates (Agazie and Hayman, 2003; Bunda et al., 2015; Klinghoffer and Kazlauskas, 1995).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: SHP099 is a potent and highly selective allosteric inhibitor of SHP2.
source: The availability of a potent and highly selective allosteric inhibitor of SHP2 now allows us to capture the whole proteome dynamics of the SHP2 dependence of the EGF response. Thus, we use here the allosteric inhibitor SHP099 (Garcia Fortanet et al., 2016) to study the role of SHP2 on phosphoprotein dynamics at the whole proteome level following EGF stimulation of a breast cancer cell line carrying an EGFR amplification.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: MDA-MB-468 is a breast cancer cell line carrying an EGFR amplification.
source: Thus, we use here the allosteric inhibitor SHP099 (Garcia Fortanet et al., 2016) to study the role of SHP2 on phosphoprotein dynamics at the whole proteome level following EGF stimulation of a breast cancer cell line carrying an EGFR amplification.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the MDA-MB-468 cell line.

claim: Putative substrate sites fall into two classes, with increased pY abundance at early and/or late timepoints.
source: Putative substrate sites fall into two classes, with increased pY abundance at early and/or late timepoints, respectively.
evidence: This is a finding from the phosphoproteomics data analysis.

claim: A class of sites exhibits decreased pY abundance and contains the largest number of dynamic pY sites.
source: Yet another class, which contains the largest number of dynamic pY sites, exhibits decreased pY abundance.
evidence: This is a finding from the phosphoproteomics data analysis.

claim: Sites with decreased pY abundance are enriched on proteins with two nearby pY residues, some of which are directly protected from dephosphorylation by the SH2 domains of SHP2.
source: These latter sites are enriched on proteins with two nearby pY residues, some of which are directly protected from dephosphorylation by the SH2 domains of SHP2.
evidence: This is a finding from the phosphoproteomics data and mutational studies.

claim: The data emphasize the two distinct and interrelated biochemical activities of SHP2: dephosphorylation and phosphosite protection.
source: These data emphasize the two distinct and interrelated biochemical activities of SHP2 – dephosphorylation and phosphosite protection – and identify specific sites relevant to the activity of SHP099 and similar molecules such as TNO155 as therapeutic lead compounds (LaMarche et al., 2020).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data.

claim: The data identify specific sites relevant to the activity of SHP099 as therapeutic lead compounds.
source: These data emphasize the two distinct and interrelated biochemical activities of SHP2 – dephosphorylation and phosphosite protection – and identify specific sites relevant to the activity of SHP099 and similar molecules such as TNO155 as therapeutic lead compounds (LaMarche et al., 2020).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data, with a citation to related work.

claim: The data identify specific sites relevant to the activity of TNO155 as therapeutic lead compounds.
source: These data emphasize the two distinct and interrelated biochemical activities of SHP2 – dephosphorylation and phosphosite protection – and identify specific sites relevant to the activity of SHP099 and similar molecules such as TNO155 as therapeutic lead compounds (LaMarche et al., 2020).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data, with a citation to related work.

claim: MDA-MB-468 is an EGFR-amplified cell line derived from a patient with triple-negative breast cancer.
source: We investigated the role of SHP2 in the responsiveness to EGF by using the EGFR-amplified cell line MDA-MB-468, derived from a patient with triple-negative breast cancer.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the MDA-MB-468 cell line.

claim: The response of the EGF receptor to EGF stimulation occurs in the 1–2 min time period.
source: Because the response of the EGF receptor to EGF stimulation occurs in the 1–2 min time period (Jadwin et al., 2016), we focused attention on the 5–30 min time window to ensure the observation of SHP2-dependent events downstream of EGF receptor stimulation.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: EGF stimulation results in a dramatic increase in phospho-ERK1/2 (p-ERK1/2) levels followed by a decline toward basal levels by 30 min.
source: Immunoblot analysis revealed the expected effect of EGF stimulation: a dramatic increase in phospho-ERK1/2 (p-ERK1/2) levels followed by a decline toward basal levels by 30 min.
evidence: This is shown in the Western blot data in Figure 1A.

claim: The induction of p-ERK1/2 is greatly attenuated by pretreatment of cells with 10 μM SHP099.
source: The induction of p-ERK1/2 was greatly attenuated by pretreatment of cells with 10 μM SHP099.
evidence: This is shown in the Western blot data in Figure 1A.

claim: SHP099 washout in the continued presence of EGF reveals p-ERK1/2 induction with a kinetic profile similar to that of EGF stimulation in the absence of drug.
source: SHP099 washout in the continued presence of EGF (condition 3) revealed p-ERK1/2 induction with a kinetic profile similar to that of EGF stimulation in the absence of drug (condition 1), showing that SHP099 inhibition of SHP2 is rapidly reversible in MDA-MB-468 cells (Figure 1A, Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is shown in the Western blot data in Figure 1A and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: SHP099 inhibition of SHP2 is rapidly reversible in MDA-MB-468 cells.
source: SHP099 washout in the continued presence of EGF (condition 3) revealed p-ERK1/2 induction with a kinetic profile similar to that of EGF stimulation in the absence of drug (condition 1), showing that SHP099 inhibition of SHP2 is rapidly reversible in MDA-MB-468 cells (Figure 1A, Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is inferred from the Western blot data showing recovery of p-ERK1/2 after washout.

claim: Principal component analysis revealed a high degree of consistency between matched samples from the two biological replicates.
source: Principal component analysis revealed a high degree of consistency between matched samples from the two biological replicates (Figure 1—figure supplement 2), which yielded relative quantification for several hundred pY-containing peptides, with good concordance between biological replicates (Figure 1C and Supplementary files 1 and 2).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: The phosphoproteomics experiment yielded relative quantification for several hundred pY-containing peptides, with good concordance between biological replicates.
source: Principal component analysis revealed a high degree of consistency between matched samples from the two biological replicates (Figure 1—figure supplement 2), which yielded relative quantification for several hundred pY-containing peptides, with good concordance between biological replicates (Figure 1C and Supplementary files 1 and 2).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1C and Supplementary files 1 and 2.

claim: The Western blot and mass spectrometry data for the dynamics of pY204 of ERK1 show the same pattern of response.
source: The Western blot (Figure 1A) and mass spectrometry data for the dynamics of pY204 of ERK1 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B) and pY187 of ERK2 (Supplementary files 1 and 2) show the same pattern of response, confirming that key pY marks associated with EGF-induced signaling events were accurately determined in the TMT experiment.
evidence: This is shown by comparing Western blot and mass spectrometry data.

claim: The Western blot and mass spectrometry data for the dynamics of pY187 of ERK2 show the same pattern of response.
source: The Western blot (Figure 1A) and mass spectrometry data for the dynamics of pY204 of ERK1 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B) and pY187 of ERK2 (Supplementary files 1 and 2) show the same pattern of response, confirming that key pY marks associated with EGF-induced signaling events were accurately determined in the TMT experiment.
evidence: This is shown by comparing Western blot and mass spectrometry data.

claim: Key pY marks associated with EGF-induced signaling events were accurately determined in the TMT experiment.
source: The Western blot (Figure 1A) and mass spectrometry data for the dynamics of pY204 of ERK1 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B) and pY187 of ERK2 (Supplementary files 1 and 2) show the same pattern of response, confirming that key pY marks associated with EGF-induced signaling events were accurately determined in the TMT experiment.
evidence: This is inferred from the concordance between Western blot and mass spectrometry data.

claim: SHP2 inhibition resulted in increased abundance of pY marks at a number of sites.
source: As anticipated, SHP2 inhibition resulted in increased abundance of pY marks at a number of sites (Figure 1—figure supplement 3A, top two rows), the expected effect of blocking a tyrosine phosphatase.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3A.

claim: A larger family of pY sites showed a decreased abundance when SHP2 is inhibited even at early time points.
source: Remarkably, however, we found an even larger family of pY sites that showed a decreased abundance when SHP2 is inhibited even at early time points (Figure 1—figure supplement 3A, bottom two rows), indicating that SHP2 inhibition had direct and/or indirect activities other than direct dephosphorylation of substrates.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3A.

claim: SHP2 inhibition has direct and/or indirect activities other than direct dephosphorylation of substrates.
source: Remarkably, however, we found an even larger family of pY sites that showed a decreased abundance when SHP2 is inhibited even at early time points (Figure 1—figure supplement 3A, bottom two rows), indicating that SHP2 inhibition had direct and/or indirect activities other than direct dephosphorylation of substrates.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation of decreased pY abundance upon SHP2 inhibition.

claim: A subset of sites was regulated (either positively or negatively) by SHP2 prior to EGF addition.
source: Additionally, SHP2 exhibited EGFR-independent regulation of a number of pY sites: a subset of sites was regulated (either positively or negatively) by SHP2 prior to EGF addition (Figure 1—figure supplement 3A, first and fourth rows), showing that SHP2 had a role in shaping the basal signaling state of these cells.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3A.

claim: SHP2 has a role in shaping the basal signaling state of MDA-MB-468 cells.
source: Additionally, SHP2 exhibited EGFR-independent regulation of a number of pY sites: a subset of sites was regulated (either positively or negatively) by SHP2 prior to EGF addition (Figure 1—figure supplement 3A, first and fourth rows), showing that SHP2 had a role in shaping the basal signaling state of these cells.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation of SHP2-dependent regulation prior to EGF addition.

claim: Motif analysis of phosphosites associated with different classes of SHP2 responsiveness did not reveal enrichment for specific motifs.
source: Motif analysis of phosphosites associated with different classes of SHP2 responsiveness did not reveal enrichment for specific motifs (residues flanking the modified tyrosine residue; Figure 1—figure supplement 3B).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3B.

claim: Sites from different regulatory classes can occur together in the same protein.
source: Remarkably, sites from different regulatory classes could even occur together in the same protein (see below), highlighting the importance of considering specific sites of phosphorylation when evaluating the impact of a phosphatase on a protein substrate.
evidence: This is observed in the phosphoproteomics data.

claim: It is important to consider specific sites of phosphorylation when evaluating the impact of a phosphatase on a protein substrate.
source: Remarkably, sites from different regulatory classes could even occur together in the same protein (see below), highlighting the importance of considering specific sites of phosphorylation when evaluating the impact of a phosphatase on a protein substrate.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the observation that different regulatory classes can occur in the same protein.

claim: Hierarchical clustering identified six kinetic profiles among the pY sites.
source: Hierarchical clustering was performed to identify groups of pY sites with similar kinetics in DMSO, SHP099, and washout conditions. Among the six kinetic profiles that emerged (Figure 2—figure supplement 1), we highlight three clusters of sites implicated in EGFR signaling and that display distinct responses to the drug (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: The first class of responses shows quantitatively increased tyrosine phosphorylation in the presence of SHP099 that rapidly disappears upon drug washout.
source: The first class of responses, which includes the regulatory subunits of PI3K, occludin, Syntaxin 4 (Figure 2B), the adapter proteins CRK and GRB2, and ARHGAP35 (also known as p190RhoGAP), among other proteins, shows quantitatively increased tyrosine phosphorylation in the presence of SHP099 that rapidly disappears upon drug washout (Figure 2A), as predicted for a SHP2 substrate.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2A and Figure 2B.

claim: The first class of responses matches the response predicted for a SHP2 substrate.
source: The first class of responses, which includes the regulatory subunits of PI3K, occludin, Syntaxin 4 (Figure 2B), the adapter proteins CRK and GRB2, and ARHGAP35 (also known as p190RhoGAP), among other proteins, shows quantitatively increased tyrosine phosphorylation in the presence of SHP099 that rapidly disappears upon drug washout (Figure 2A), as predicted for a SHP2 substrate.
evidence: This is inferred from the pattern of increased pY with inhibitor and decrease upon washout.

claim: The second class of sites accumulates pY marks slowly under SHP099 inhibition (at 30 min after EGF treatment), and not when SHP099 is omitted or washed out.
source: The second class of sites accumulates pY marks slowly under SHP099 inhibition (at 30 min after EGF treatment), and not when SHP099 is omitted or washed out.
evidence: This is shown in the phosphoproteomics data.

claim: The second class of sites includes pY sites on CBL E3 ligase, RAB10, hnRNPs, PLCγ proteins, and CAPRIN1.
source: This pattern, observed for pY sites on CBL E3 ligase, RAB10, hnRNPs, PLCγ proteins, and CAPRIN1 (Figure 2C), also matches the response predicted for a SHP2 substrate, but with a time delay, suggesting that the action of SHP2 on these proteins might require an intervening event, such as relocalization (e.g. after endocytosis of active EGFR signaling complexes), or alternatively, that the effect is indirect.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The second class of sites matches the response predicted for a SHP2 substrate, but with a time delay.
source: This pattern, observed for pY sites on CBL E3 ligase, RAB10, hnRNPs, PLCγ proteins, and CAPRIN1 (Figure 2C), also matches the response predicted for a SHP2 substrate, but with a time delay, suggesting that the action of SHP2 on these proteins might require an intervening event, such as relocalization (e.g. after endocytosis of active EGFR signaling complexes), or alternatively, that the effect is indirect.
evidence: This is inferred from the delayed accumulation of pY marks.

claim: The action of SHP2 on the second class of sites might require an intervening event, such as relocalization.
source: This pattern, observed for pY sites on CBL E3 ligase, RAB10, hnRNPs, PLCγ proteins, and CAPRIN1 (Figure 2C), also matches the response predicted for a SHP2 substrate, but with a time delay, suggesting that the action of SHP2 on these proteins might require an intervening event, such as relocalization (e.g. after endocytosis of active EGFR signaling complexes), or alternatively, that the effect is indirect.
evidence: This is speculation based on the delayed response pattern.

claim: The effect of SHP2 on the second class of sites might be indirect.
source: This pattern, observed for pY sites on CBL E3 ligase, RAB10, hnRNPs, PLCγ proteins, and CAPRIN1 (Figure 2C), also matches the response predicted for a SHP2 substrate, but with a time delay, suggesting that the action of SHP2 on these proteins might require an intervening event, such as relocalization (e.g. after endocytosis of active EGFR signaling complexes), or alternatively, that the effect is indirect.
evidence: This is speculation based on the delayed response pattern.

claim: SHP2 may catalyze dephosphorylation of many different proteins on different time scales.
source: The large number of potential substrates identified in this work suggests that SHP2 may catalyze dephosphorylation of many different proteins on different time scales.
evidence: This is inferred from the identification of multiple substrate classes with different kinetics.

claim: The third pattern of response is one in which accumulation of pY in response to EGF depends on the release of SHP2 from inhibition by SHP099.
source: The third pattern of response observed is one in which accumulation of pY in response to EGF depends on the release of SHP2 from inhibition by SHP099.
evidence: This is shown in the phosphoproteomics data.

claim: Y1100 of ARHGEF5 falls into the third pattern of response.
source: Examples of sites that fall into this category include Y1100 of ARHGEF5 (Figure 2D), Y659 of GAB1, Y643 of GAB2, as well as Y546 and Y584 of SHP2 itself.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Y659 of GAB1 falls into the third pattern of response.
source: Examples of sites that fall into this category include Y1100 of ARHGEF5 (Figure 2D), Y659 of GAB1, Y643 of GAB2, as well as Y546 and Y584 of SHP2 itself.
evidence: This is shown in the phosphoproteomics data.

claim: Y643 of GAB2 falls into the third pattern of response.
source: Examples of sites that fall into this category include Y1100 of ARHGEF5 (Figure 2D), Y659 of GAB1, Y643 of GAB2, as well as Y546 and Y584 of SHP2 itself.
evidence: This is shown in the phosphoproteomics data.

claim: Y546 of SHP2 falls into the third pattern of response.
source: Examples of sites that fall into this category include Y1100 of ARHGEF5 (Figure 2D), Y659 of GAB1, Y643 of GAB2, as well as Y546 and Y584 of SHP2 itself.
evidence: This is shown in the phosphoproteomics data.

claim: Y584 of SHP2 falls into the third pattern of response.
source: Examples of sites that fall into this category include Y1100 of ARHGEF5 (Figure 2D), Y659 of GAB1, Y643 of GAB2, as well as Y546 and Y584 of SHP2 itself.
evidence: This is shown in the phosphoproteomics data.

claim: Proteins implicated in MAPK and PI3K signaling contain numerous EGF-responsive phosphosites differentially regulated by SHP099 treatment.
source: As expected, proteins implicated in MAPK and PI3K signaling, including EGFR and SHP2 itself, contain numerous EGF-responsive phosphosites differentially regulated by SHP099 treatment.
evidence: This is shown in the functional classification analysis in Figure 2—figure supplement 2D.

claim: The largest functional group includes proteins implicated in adhesion and migration.
source: The largest functional group includes proteins implicated in adhesion and migration, including tight junction proteins, catenins, Rho-GEF, and Rho-GAP proteins.
evidence: This is shown in the functional classification analysis.

claim: SHP2 promotes migration in MDA-MB-468 cells by regulating EGF-induced lamellipodia persistence.
source: These findings, along with data on the abundance of cytoskeletal proteins differentially affected by SHP099 (Figure 2—figure supplement 2D), are consistent with earlier results, suggesting that SHP2 promotes migration in MDA-MB-468 cells by regulating EGF-induced lamellipodia persistence (Hartman et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work and is consistent with the current data.

claim: Proteins implicated in transcription comprise another functional class with a number of differentially regulated phosphosites.
source: Proteins implicated in transcription comprise another functional class with a number of differentially regulated phosphosites (Figure 2—figure supplement 2D).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2D.

claim: Endocytosis and mRNA processing have not previously been linked to SHP2 activity.
source: Two additional functional categories enriched in the analysis comprise endocytosis and mRNA processing, neither of which have previously been linked to SHP2 activity.
evidence: This is a statement about the novelty of the findings.

claim: Most of the sites in the endocytosis and mRNA processing categories display a substrate-like response with SHP099 treatment.
source: Most of the sites in these two categories display a substrate-like response with SHP099 treatment.
evidence: This is shown in the phosphoproteomics data.

claim: SHP099 affects phosphorylation of CBL and CBLB, E3 ligases that ubiquitinate EGFR and facilitate its recruitment to clathrin-coated pits for endocytosis.
source: In addition, SHP099 also affected phosphorylation of CBL and CBLB, E3 ligases that ubiquitinate EGFR and facilitate its recruitment to clathrin-coated pits for endocytosis.
evidence: This is shown in the phosphoproteomics data, and the function of CBL and CBLB is established knowledge.

claim: The results highlight the diversity of influence of SHP2, both in the function of proteins that it affects and in the manner in which it affects their phosphorylation patterns.
source: Together, these results highlight the diversity of influence of SHP2, both in the function of proteins that it affects and in the manner in which it affects their phosphorylation patterns.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the phosphoproteomics data.

claim: Only one of the phosphosites observed with a substrate-like pattern has previously been reported to be dephosphorylated by SHP2 (GRB2 pY209).
source: Among proteins that show a substrate-like pattern, only one of the phosphosites observed has previously been reported to be dephosphorylated by SHP2 (GRB2 pY209; ARHGAP35 has also been reported to be a substrate, but its pY site has not been reported) (Bregeon et al., 2009; Chardin et al., 1993).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: ARHGAP35 has been reported to be a SHP2 substrate, but its pY site has not been reported.
source: Among proteins that show a substrate-like pattern, only one of the phosphosites observed has previously been reported to be dephosphorylated by SHP2 (GRB2 pY209; ARHGAP35 has also been reported to be a substrate, but its pY site has not been reported) (Bregeon et al., 2009; Chardin et al., 1993).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Three proteins (occludin, PLCγ2, and ARHGAP35) that were reliably immunoprecipitated at endogenous abundance showed phosphosite enrichment after EGF stimulation in the presence of SHP099.
source: Of these twenty proteins screened (Supplementary file 3), three that were reliably immunoprecipiated at endogenous abundance showed phosphosite enrichment after EGF stimulation in the presence of SHP099 as judged by Western blot with an anti-pY antibody. These three proteins are occludin, PLCγ2, and ARHGAGP35 (Figure 3A–C).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3A–C.

claim: PLCγ2, occludin, and GRB2 accumulate pY in the presence of SHP099 when immunoprecipitated with an anti-pY antibody in EGF-stimulated cells.
source: Immunoprecipitation of pY-modified proteins with an anti-pY antibody in EGF-stimulated cells treated with SHP099 likewise showed that PLCγ2, occludin, and GRB2 accumulate pY in the presence of SHP099, as judged by Western blot (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Accumulation of the pY1105 mark on ARHGAP35 occurs when SHP2 is inhibited by SHP099.
source: Because it was not possible to immunoprecipitate ARHGAP35 with either the anti-pY antibody or an antibody that specifically reognizes the pY1105 phosphosite, we immunoblotted anti-ARHGAP35 immunoprecipitates with the anti-pY1105 antibody to confirm that accumulation of this specific mark occurs when SHP2 is inhibited by SHP099 (Figure 3D,E).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3D,E.

claim: SHP2 can robustly remove the phosphate mark from pY209 of GRB2.
source: In addition, enzyme assays using purified SHP2 and the pY-containing peptides that contain the SHP099-enriched phsophosites identified in the proteomic studies confirm that SHP2 can robustly remove the phosphate mark from pY209 of GRB2, pY443 of occludin, pY1105 of ARHGAP35, and pY818 of PLCγ2, whereas neither a control peptide containing pY708 from CSF-1R nor a Class III peptide from TMEM134 that shows a protection-type pattern are robust SHP2 substrates (Figure 3F).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3F.

claim: SHP2 can robustly remove the phosphate mark from pY443 of occludin.
source: In addition, enzyme assays using purified SHP2 and the pY-containing peptides that contain the SHP099-enriched phsophosites identified in the proteomic studies confirm that SHP2 can robustly remove the phosphate mark from pY209 of GRB2, pY443 of occludin, pY1105 of ARHGAP35, and pY818 of PLCγ2, whereas neither a control peptide containing pY708 from CSF-1R nor a Class III peptide from TMEM134 that shows a protection-type pattern are robust SHP2 substrates (Figure 3F).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3F.

claim: SHP2 can robustly remove the phosphate mark from pY1105 of ARHGAP35.

evidence: This is shown in Figure 3F.

claim: SHP2 can robustly remove the phosphate mark from pY818 of PLCγ2.
source: In addition, enzyme assays using purified SHP2 and the pY-containing peptides that contain the SHP099-enriched phsophosites identified in the proteomic studies confirm that SHP2 can robustly remove the phosphate mark from pY209 of GRB2, pY443 of occludin, pY1105 of ARHGAP35, and pY818 of PLCγ2, whereas neither a control peptide containing pY708 from CSF-1R nor a Class III peptide from TMEM134 that shows a protection-type pattern are robust SHP2 substrates (Figure 3F).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3F.

claim: A control peptide containing pY708 from CSF-1R is not a robust SHP2 substrate.
source: In addition, enzyme assays using purified SHP2 and the pY-containing peptides that contain the SHP099-enriched phsophosites identified in the proteomic studies confirm that SHP2 can robustly remove the phosphate mark from pY209 of GRB2, pY443 of occludin, pY1105 of ARHGAP35, and pY818 of PLCγ2, whereas neither a control peptide containing pY708 from CSF-1R nor a Class III peptide from TMEM134 that shows a protection-type pattern are robust SHP2 substrates (Figure 3F).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3F.

claim: A Class III peptide from TMEM134 that shows a protection-type pattern is not a robust SHP2 substrate.
source: In addition, enzyme assays using purified SHP2 and the pY-containing peptides that contain the SHP099-enriched phsophosites identified in the proteomic studies confirm that SHP2 can robustly remove the phosphate mark from pY209 of GRB2, pY443 of occludin, pY1105 of ARHGAP35, and pY818 of PLCγ2, whereas neither a control peptide containing pY708 from CSF-1R nor a Class III peptide from TMEM134 that shows a protection-type pattern are robust SHP2 substrates (Figure 3F).

claim: ARHGAP35, PLCγ2, and occludin are newly identified substrates for SHP2 in EGF-stimulated MDA-MB-468 cells.
source: Together, these data suggest that ARHGAP35, PLCγ2, and occludin are newly identified substrates for SHP2 in EGF-stimulated MDA-MB-468 cells.
evidence: This is inferred from the immunoprecipitation and enzyme assay data.

claim: SHP099 allosterically stabilizes the autoinhibited conformation of SHP2.
source: SHP099 allosterically stabilizes the autoinhibited conformation of SHP2 (Chen et al., 2016), thereby not only inhibiting the catalytic activity of the enzyme, but also suppressing binding of its two SH2 domains to pY-containing motifs.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: SHP099 inhibits the catalytic activity of SHP2.
source: SHP099 allosterically stabilizes the autoinhibited conformation of SHP2 (Chen et al., 2016), thereby not only inhibiting the catalytic activity of the enzyme, but also suppressing binding of its two SH2 domains to pY-containing motifs.
evidence: This is established knowledge about SHP099 mechanism.

claim: SHP099 suppresses binding of the two SH2 domains of SHP2 to pY-containing motifs.
source: SHP099 allosterically stabilizes the autoinhibited conformation of SHP2 (Chen et al., 2016), thereby not only inhibiting the catalytic activity of the enzyme, but also suppressing binding of its two SH2 domains to pY-containing motifs.
evidence: This is inferred from the mechanism of allosteric stabilization of the autoinhibited conformation.

claim: Y659 of GAB1 shows dramatic reductions in pY abundance upon SHP099 treatment.
source: Y659 of GAB1 and Y643 of GAB2 both show dramatic reductions in pY abundance upon SHP099 treatment and recover their pY marks upon compound washout (Figure 4), as judged by the phosphoproteomic data and confirmed across an extended time course by Western blot.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4.

claim: Y643 of GAB2 shows dramatic reductions in pY abundance upon SHP099 treatment.
source: Y659 of GAB1 and Y643 of GAB2 both show dramatic reductions in pY abundance upon SHP099 treatment and recover their pY marks upon compound washout (Figure 4), as judged by the phosphoproteomic data and confirmed across an extended time course by Western blot.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4.

claim: Y659 of GAB1 and Y643 of GAB2 recover their pY marks upon SHP099 washout.
source: Y659 of GAB1 and Y643 of GAB2 both show dramatic reductions in pY abundance upon SHP099 treatment and recover their pY marks upon compound washout (Figure 4), as judged by the phosphoproteomic data and confirmed across an extended time course by Western blot.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4.

claim: The SH2 domains of SHP2 can bind to the bisphosphotyrosine-containing motifs of GAB1 (pY627/pY659) to relieve SHP2 autoinhibition.
source: These data are fully consistent with prior work indicating that the SH2 domains of SHP2 can bind to the bisphosphotyrosine-containing motifs of GAB1 (pY627/pY659) and GAB2 (pY614/pY643) to relieve SHP2 autoinhibition (Arnaud et al., 2004; Cunnick et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work and is consistent with the current data.

claim: The SH2 domains of SHP2 can bind to the bisphosphotyrosine-containing motifs of GAB2 (pY614/pY643) to relieve SHP2 autoinhibition.
source: These data are fully consistent with prior work indicating that the SH2 domains of SHP2 can bind to the bisphosphotyrosine-containing motifs of GAB1 (pY627/pY659) and GAB2 (pY614/pY643) to relieve SHP2 autoinhibition (Arnaud et al., 2004; Cunnick et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work and is consistent with the current data.

claim: KYSE520 is an EGFR-amplified esophageal cancer cell line.
source: KYSE520, an EGFR-amplified esophageal cancer cell line, showed loss of GAB1 Y659 phosphorylation with SHP099 treatment under conditions of EGF stimulation (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is established knowledge about the KYSE520 cell line.

claim: KYSE520 showed loss of GAB1 Y659 phosphorylation with SHP099 treatment under conditions of EGF stimulation.
source: KYSE520, an EGFR-amplified esophageal cancer cell line, showed loss of GAB1 Y659 phosphorylation with SHP099 treatment under conditions of EGF stimulation (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claim: H1975 cells carry an EGFR activating mutation.
source: H1975 cells, which carry an EGFR activating mutation, displayed high levels of constitutive GAB2-Y643 phosphorylation.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the H1975 cell line.

claim: H1975 cells display high levels of constitutive GAB2-Y643 phosphorylation.
source: H1975 cells, which carry an EGFR activating mutation, displayed high levels of constitutive GAB2-Y643 phosphorylation.
evidence: This is shown in the Western blot data.

claim: SHP099 treatment eliminates phosphorylation of GAB2-Y643 in H1975 cells.
source: SHP099 treatment eliminated phosphorylation of this site, and washout of the drug restores the mark within 5 min (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Washout of SHP099 restores the GAB2-Y643 mark within 5 min in H1975 cells.
source: SHP099 treatment eliminated phosphorylation of this site, and washout of the drug restores the mark within 5 min (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B.

claim: SHP2-null U2OS cells show a reduction in GAB1 pY659 levels when compared to parental cells when stimulated with EGF.
source: When stimulated with EGF, SHP2-null U2OS cells showed a reduction in GAB1 pY659 levels when compared to parental cells, and reintroduction of SHP2 fully rescued the level of accumulated pY659 (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Reintroduction of SHP2 fully rescues the level of accumulated GAB1 pY659 in SHP2-null U2OS cells.
source: When stimulated with EGF, SHP2-null U2OS cells showed a reduction in GAB1 pY659 levels when compared to parental cells, and reintroduction of SHP2 fully rescued the level of accumulated pY659 (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Stimulation of U2OS cells with PDGFββ induces the GAB1 pY659 mark that is lost upon treatment with SHP099.
source: Stimulation of U2OS cells with PDGFββ also showed an induction of the GAB1 pY659 mark that is lost upon treatment with SHP099 (Figure 4—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Stimulation of the T cell receptor on Jurkat cells with an anti-CD3 antibody induces GAB1 and GAB2 phosphorylation.
source: Similarly, stimulation of the T cell receptor on Jurkat cells with an anti-CD3 antibody induced GAB1 and GAB2 phosphorylation, and this induction was attenuated by SHP099 treatment (Figure 4—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1E.

claim: Induction of GAB1 and GAB2 phosphorylation by anti-CD3 antibody in Jurkat cells is attenuated by SHP099 treatment.
source: Similarly, stimulation of the T cell receptor on Jurkat cells with an anti-CD3 antibody induced GAB1 and GAB2 phosphorylation, and this induction was attenuated by SHP099 treatment (Figure 4—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1E.

claim: The effect of SHP2 on the abundance of GAB1 and GAB2 pY marks is broadly shared among a range of growth factor and antigen receptor signaling systems.
source: These findings show that the effect of SHP2 on the abundance of GAB1 and GAB2 pY marks is broadly shared among a range of growth factor and antigen receptor signaling systems.
evidence: This is inferred from the data in multiple cell lines and stimulation conditions.

claim: C459E, E76K, and the E76K/C459E double mutant all restore GAB1-pY659 phosphorylation to a level similar to that of cells rescued with wild-type SHP2 when stimulated with EGF.
source: When stimulated with EGF, C459E, E76K, and the E76K/C459E double mutant, all restored GAB1-pY659 phosphorylation to a level similar to that of cells rescued with wild-type SHP2 (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5B.

claim: The PTP fragment of SHP2 fails to rescue GAB1-pY659 phosphorylation in U2OS cells lacking endogenous SHP2.
source: When the SH2 or PTP constructs were introduced into U2OS cells lacking endogenous SHP2, the PTP fragment failed to rescue, whereas the SH2 fragment was as active as wild-type SHP2 (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5C.

claim: The SH2 fragment of SHP2 is as active as wild-type SHP2 in rescuing GAB1-pY659 phosphorylation in U2OS cells lacking endogenous SHP2.
source: When the SH2 or PTP constructs were introduced into U2OS cells lacking endogenous SHP2, the PTP fragment failed to rescue, whereas the SH2 fragment was as active as wild-type SHP2 (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5C.

claim: The SH2 fragment, but not the PTP fragment, is active in increasing pY abundance at GAB1 and GAB2 positions in MDA-MB-468 cells when endogenous SHP2 is chemically inhibited.
source: Consistent with the results from U2OS cells, the SH2 fragment, but not the PTP fragment was active in increasing pY abundance at these positions of GAB1 and GAB2 (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5D.

claim: The SH2 fragment stabilizes GAB1 and GAB2 phospho marks even in the absence of EGF stimulation.
source: Indeed, the SH2 fragment stabilizes these GAB1 and GAB2 phospho marks even in the absence of EGF stimulation (Figure 5D), consistent with a dominant protective function that is independent of the catalytic activity of the enzyme.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5D.

claim: The SH2 fragment has a dominant protective function that is independent of the catalytic activity of SHP2.
source: Indeed, the SH2 fragment stabilizes these GAB1 and GAB2 phospho marks even in the absence of EGF stimulation (Figure 5D), consistent with a dominant protective function that is independent of the catalytic activity of the enzyme.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that the SH2 fragment stabilizes phospho marks without catalytic activity.

claim: The SHP099-resistant variant of SHP2 (T253M/Q257L) rescues protection of the GAB1 and GAB2 pY sites.
source: In addition, the SHP099-resistant variant of SHP2 (T253M/Q257L) rescues protection of the GAB1 and GAB2 pY sites (Figure 6A,B), and point mutation of the key arginine residue of each SH2 domain (R32M of the N-SH2 domain or R138M of the C-SH2 domain) suppresses phosphosite protection of these sites, as does the R32M/R138M double mutant (Figure 6C,D).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6A,B.

claim: Point mutation of R32M of the N-SH2 domain suppresses phosphosite protection of GAB1 and GAB2 sites.
source: In addition, the SHP099-resistant variant of SHP2 (T253M/Q257L) rescues protection of the GAB1 and GAB2 pY sites (Figure 6A,B), and point mutation of the key arginine residue of each SH2 domain (R32M of the N-SH2 domain or R138M of the C-SH2 domain) suppresses phosphosite protection of these sites, as does the R32M/R138M double mutant (Figure 6C,D).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6C,D.

claim: Point mutation of R138M of the C-SH2 domain suppresses phosphosite protection of GAB1 and GAB2 sites.
source: In addition, the SHP099-resistant variant of SHP2 (T253M/Q257L) rescues protection of the GAB1 and GAB2 pY sites (Figure 6A,B), and point mutation of the key arginine residue of each SH2 domain (R32M of the N-SH2 domain or R138M of the C-SH2 domain) suppresses phosphosite protection of these sites, as does the R32M/R138M double mutant (Figure 6C,D).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6C,D.

claim: The R32M/R138M double mutant suppresses phosphosite protection of GAB1 and GAB2 sites.
source: In addition, the SHP099-resistant variant of SHP2 (T253M/Q257L) rescues protection of the GAB1 and GAB2 pY sites (Figure 6A,B), and point mutation of the key arginine residue of each SH2 domain (R32M of the N-SH2 domain or R138M of the C-SH2 domain) suppresses phosphosite protection of these sites, as does the R32M/R138M double mutant (Figure 6C,D).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6C,D.

claim: The catalytic activity of SHP2 is not required for the protection of the pY659 and pY643 marks on GAB1 and GAB2, respectively.
source: Together, these findings show that the catalytic activity of SHP2 is not required for the protection of the pY659 and pY643 marks on GAB1 and GAB2, respectively, and argue that the presence of tandem SH2 domains in SHP2 is needed to bind and protect pYs on GAB1 and GAB2 from phosphatase-mediated dephosphorylation.
evidence: This is inferred from the mutational studies showing that catalytically inactive mutants can still protect these sites.

claim: The presence of tandem SH2 domains in SHP2 is needed to bind and protect pYs on GAB1 and GAB2 from phosphatase-mediated dephosphorylation.
source: Together, these findings show that the catalytic activity of SHP2 is not required for the protection of the pY659 and pY643 marks on GAB1 and GAB2, respectively, and argue that the presence of tandem SH2 domains in SHP2 is needed to bind and protect pYs on GAB1 and GAB2 from phosphatase-mediated dephosphorylation.
evidence: This is inferred from the mutational studies showing that SH2 domains are necessary for protection.

claim: MPZL1 is a cell surface receptor involved in extracellular matrix-induced signaling.
source: To assess whether this protection mechanism applies to other SHP2 interacting proteins that show reduced pY abundance in the presence of SHP099, we studied MPZL1, a cell surface receptor involved in extracellular matrix-induced signaling (Beigbeder et al., 2017; Zhao et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: MPZL1 contains an immunoreceptor tyrosine-based inhibitory motif (ITIM) that, when doubly phosphorylated at Y241 and Y263, can bind the tandem SH2 domains of SHP2.
source: MPZL1 contains an immunoreceptor tyrosine-based inhibitory motif (ITIM) that, when doubly phosphorylated at Y241 and Y263, can bind the tandem SH2 domains of SHP2 (Zhao and Zhao, 2000).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Basal pY abundance at Y241 and Y263 of MPZL1 is greatly reduced by SHP099 treatment.
source: Our phosphoproteomic data show that basal pY abundance at these sites is greatly reduced by SHP099 treatment and that the dependence of pY modifications on SHP2 at these two sites occurs independent of EGF (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A,B.

claim: The dependence of pY modifications on SHP2 at Y241 and Y263 of MPZL1 occurs independent of EGF.
source: Our phosphoproteomic data show that basal pY abundance at these sites is greatly reduced by SHP099 treatment and that the dependence of pY modifications on SHP2 at these two sites occurs independent of EGF (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A,B.

claim: The tandem SH2 domains alone are sufficient to protect the phosphate groups on Y241 and Y263 of MPZL1.
source: Using immunoblot assays, we found that the tandem SH2 domains alone are also sufficient to protect the phosphate groups on Y241 and Y263 of MPZL1 (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1C.

claim: The two pY sites on the SHP2 C-terminal tail exhibit a protection-type pattern in the presence of SHP099.
source: It is also notable that the two pY sites on the SHP2 C-terminal tail exhibit a protection-type pattern in the presence of SHP099.
evidence: This is observed in the phosphoproteomics data.

claim: The allosteric inhibitor SHP099 interferes with membrane recruitment of SHP2 by preventing the SH2 domains from binding to pY residues deposited at membrane proximal sites by activated kinases.
source: Because the allosteric inhibitor locks SHP2 in the closed conformation, we speculate that the inhibitor interferes with membrane recruitment of SHP2 by preventing the SH2 domains from binding to pY residues deposited at membrane proximal sites by activated kinases and that removal of inhibitor permits membrane recruitment to sites of EGFR activation, phosphorylation of the SHP2 C-terminal tail, and subsequent GRB2 recruitment.
evidence: This is speculation based on the mechanism of SHP099 and the observed data.

claim: Removal of SHP099 permits membrane recruitment of SHP2 to sites of EGFR activation, phosphorylation of the SHP2 C-terminal tail, and subsequent GRB2 recruitment.
source: Because the allosteric inhibitor locks SHP2 in the closed conformation, we speculate that the inhibitor interferes with membrane recruitment of SHP2 by preventing the SH2 domains from binding to pY residues deposited at membrane proximal sites by activated kinases and that removal of inhibitor permits membrane recruitment to sites of EGFR activation, phosphorylation of the SHP2 C-terminal tail, and subsequent GRB2 recruitment.
evidence: This is speculation based on the mechanism of SHP099 and the observed data.

claim: GAB1, GAB2, and MPZL1 can be phosphorylated by Src family kinases (SFKs).
source: Multiple studies have reported that GAB1, GAB2, and MPZL1 can be phosphorylated by Src family kinases (SFKs) (Chan et al., 2003; Kong et al., 2003; Kusano et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: MDA-MB-468 cells treated with an SFK inhibitor (saracatinib/AZD0530) show greatly reduced modification of GAB1-Y659 and GAB2-Y643.
source: Indeed, MDA-MB-468 cells treated with an SFK inhibitor (saracatinib/AZD0530) showed greatly reduced modification of GAB1-Y659 and GAB2-Y643 (Figure 5—figure supplement 2A), suggesting that SFK activity is required to phosphorylate the SHP2 binding sites on GAB1 and GAB2.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2A.

claim: SFK activity is required to phosphorylate the SHP2 binding sites on GAB1 and GAB2.
source: Indeed, MDA-MB-468 cells treated with an SFK inhibitor (saracatinib/AZD0530) showed greatly reduced modification of GAB1-Y659 and GAB2-Y643 (Figure 5—figure supplement 2A), suggesting that SFK activity is required to phosphorylate the SHP2 binding sites on GAB1 and GAB2.
evidence: This is inferred from the effect of SFK inhibition on GAB1 and GAB2 phosphorylation.

claim: SHP099 has no detectable effect on the abundance of pY at Y416 of the activation loop of SFKs.
source: SHP099, however, had no detectable effect on the abundance of pY at Y416 of the activation loop of SFKs (Figure 5—figure supplement 2B), or on the abundance of pY at Y527, which maintains SFKs in their autoinhibitory conformation (Roskoski, 2005).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2B.

claim: SHP099 has no detectable effect on the abundance of pY at Y527 of SFKs, which maintains SFKs in their autoinhibitory conformation.
source: SHP099, however, had no detectable effect on the abundance of pY at Y416 of the activation loop of SFKs (Figure 5—figure supplement 2B), or on the abundance of pY at Y527, which maintains SFKs in their autoinhibitory conformation (Roskoski, 2005).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2B, and the function of Y527 is supported by a citation.

claim: SHP2 acts to increase the half-life of pY modifications at sites on GAB1 and GAB2 that are phosphorylated by SFKs and then bound by SHP2.
source: Although it is possible that SFK activity in the GAB complex is not reflected by assessment of bulk SFK activity in the whole-ell lysate, when combined with the phosphosite protection results from the studies with various forms of SHP2 above, these data suggest that SHP2 acts to increase the half-life of pY modifications at sites on GAB1 and GAB2 that are phosphorylated by SFKs and then bound by SHP2.
evidence: This is inferred from the combined data on SFK activity and SHP2 protection.

claim: Within 2 min of EGF addition, cells treated with DMSO alone display a strong PLA signal indicative of GAB1 and EGFR co-localization.
source: Under serum-starved (basal) conditions, the PLA signal was minimal and unaffected by SHP2 inhibition with SHP099. In contrast, within 2 min of EGF addition, cells treated with DMSO alone displayed a strong PLA signal indicative of GAB1 and EGFR co-localization, whereas SHP099 treatment reduced the number of binding events by 85% (p<0.05; Figure 5—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 3.

claim: SHP099 treatment reduces the number of GAB1-EGFR binding events by 85%.
source: Under serum-starved (basal) conditions, the PLA signal was minimal and unaffected by SHP2 inhibition with SHP099. In contrast, within 2 min of EGF addition, cells treated with DMSO alone displayed a strong PLA signal indicative of GAB1 and EGFR co-localization, whereas SHP099 treatment reduced the number of binding events by 85% (p<0.05; Figure 5—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 3.

claim: SHP2 is required to assemble the EGFR-GAB1 signaling hub crucial for MAPK and PI3K signaling.
source: These results suggest that SHP2 is required to assemble the EGFR-GAB1 signaling hub crucial for MAPK and PI3K signaling.
evidence: This is inferred from the PLA data showing reduced EGFR-GAB1 co-localization with SHP2 inhibition.

claim: The scaffolding function of SHP2 is central at the EGFR signaling hub and in the engagement of pY sites on GAB1 and GAB2 at the site of activation.
source: The work reported here shows how central the scaffolding function is at the EGFR signaling hub and in the engagement of pY sites on GAB1 and GAB2 at the site of activation, with the phosphatase-dependent events, through adapter proteins like Grb2 and key signaling nodes like PI3K, required for full propagation of a growth factor induced signal to downstream effectors.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data.

claim: Phosphatase-dependent events, through adapter proteins like Grb2 and key signaling nodes like PI3K, are required for full propagation of a growth factor induced signal to downstream effectors.
source: The work reported here shows how central the scaffolding function is at the EGFR signaling hub and in the engagement of pY sites on GAB1 and GAB2 at the site of activation, with the phosphatase-dependent events, through adapter proteins like Grb2 and key signaling nodes like PI3K, required for full propagation of a growth factor induced signal to downstream effectors.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data.

claim: Noonan syndrome mutations destabilize the autoinhibited form of SHP2 without substantially affecting the intrinsic catalytic activity of the phosphatase domain.
source: Mutations found in Noonan syndrome destabilize the autoinhibited form of the enzyme without substantially affecting the intrinsic catalytic activity of the phosphatase domain, leading to increased basal phosphatase activity, elevated scaffolding activity, and downstream induction of ERK (Araki et al., 2004; Niihori et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Noonan syndrome mutations lead to increased basal phosphatase activity, elevated scaffolding activity, and downstream induction of ERK.
source: Mutations found in Noonan syndrome destabilize the autoinhibited form of the enzyme without substantially affecting the intrinsic catalytic activity of the phosphatase domain, leading to increased basal phosphatase activity, elevated scaffolding activity, and downstream induction of ERK (Araki et al., 2004; Niihori et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: LEOPARD syndrome mutations destabilize the autoinhibited conformation of SHP2 and cripple the catalytic activity of the phosphatase domain.
source: LEOPARD syndrome mutations also destabilize the autoinhibited conformation of the enzyme, enhancing scaffolding activity, but in addition cripple the catalytic activity of the phosphatase domain.
evidence: This is established knowledge about LEOPARD syndrome mutations.

claim: The increased preference for the open conformation in both Noonan and LEOPARD syndrome mutations promotes the protective 'arm' of SHP2 signaling.
source: The increased preference for the open conformation in both Noonan and LEOPARD syndrome mutations promotes the protective 'arm' of SHP2 signaling, whereas only Noonan syndrome mutations retain the catalytic activity needed to drive the substrate-dependent features of signaling.
evidence: This is inferred from the known effects of these mutations and the data in this study.

claim: Only Noonan syndrome mutations retain the catalytic activity needed to drive the substrate-dependent features of signaling.
source: The increased preference for the open conformation in both Noonan and LEOPARD syndrome mutations promotes the protective 'arm' of SHP2 signaling, whereas only Noonan syndrome mutations retain the catalytic activity needed to drive the substrate-dependent features of signaling.
evidence: This is inferred from the known effects of these mutations.
